subtitulo: The bourgeoisie that formed outside the country and financed the nation (1774 – 1821), and the one that in 2026 still doesn't pay taxes

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for

items.text: First, in Corfu, the Spianada. Walk across it knowing that this is where the Golden Book was burned in 1797, that four flags paraded across it in eighteen years, and that today it is a cricket pitch ringed with cafés. Few public spaces pack this much constitutional history into so few square meters.

Second, the Kapodistrias Museum in Evropouli and, time permitting, the building of the Ionian Academy. Kapodistrias is the hinge figure of this entire project: a European-educated Corfiot, minister of a foreign empire, first ruler of Greece, assassinated by local notables he had tried to bring under state control. His biography is, quite literally, the thesis of entregas 11 and 12.

Third, in Athens, look at the surnames. The country's most important cultural foundations — Onassis, Niarchos, Latsis — bear the names of shipowners, and the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center, opened in 2016 with the National Opera and the National Library inside it, was built with private money and donated to the state during the harshest years of the crisis. Visit it if you can: it is a remarkable Renzo Piano building and it is also entrega 5's evergetism in its twenty-first-century form. Herodes Atticus financed an odeon; Niarchos financed an opera house. In both cases, private wealth producing a public good and, with it, a permanent place in the city's memory and an unassailable position. Ask yourself what that buys, and what it takes off the table for discussion.

sections.heading: A technical clause that created a social class
paragraphs: The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774 allowed the merchant ships of Orthodox Ottoman subjects to sail under the Russian flag. Read as diplomatic history it is a footnote. Read as social history it is the founding act of the modern Greek bourgeoisie. Under the Russian flag, those ships fell outside Ottoman taxation, were protected by a European power, and gained access to the Black Sea ports that Russia had just opened to international trade.

Twenty years later an unrepeatable conjuncture was added to this. Between 1793 and 1815, the revolutionary and Napoleonic wars withdrew the French, British, and Dutch merchant marines from the Mediterranean, occupied or blockaded as they were. Neutrals filled the vacuum. Shipowners from three small islands in the Saronic Gulf — Hydra, Spetses, and Psara, arid islands with no agriculture, largely populated by Albanian-speaking Arvanites — made fortunes carrying Russian grain to a hungry Europe, and running blockades when the price justified it. By 1813, Hydra alone had more than a hundred large armed vessels, crewed by experienced sailors accustomed to defending themselves.

When the revolution broke out in 1821, that merchant fleet became the Greek navy, initially financed by its own owners. Greek independence at sea was made by private entrepreneurs with their own ships and their own money, which also explains one of the chronic conflicts of the revolutionary period: the shipowners demanded compensation, and when public money ran short, the naval war stopped. The nation was not only an ideal; it was also an investment expecting a return.

sections.heading: A nation imagined from Odessa, Vienna, and Trieste
paragraphs: The second piece is the commercial diaspora. Over the course of the eighteenth century, Greek merchant colonies consolidated in Odessa — founded in 1794, where Greeks were the dominant commercial group in its first decades —, Vienna, Trieste, Livorno, Marseille, Amsterdam, Alexandria, and later London and Manchester, where houses such as that of the Ralli brothers operated on a global scale. These were family networks, with credit resting on intracommunal trust, capable of moving goods and information across rival empires.

These networks financed culture before politics: printing presses in Vienna publishing in Greek, the first Greek-language newspaper — the Efimerís, Vienna, 1790 —, schools, scholarships, translations. And they later financed the conspiracy: the Filikí Etaireía was founded in Odessa in 1814 among merchants of middling rank, not among aristocrats or peasants.

The central sociological observation of this entrega is this: the bourgeoisie that produced Greek nationalism formed OUTSIDE THE NATIONAL TERRITORY, inside foreign imperial economies, and its nationalism was in part a response to a structural ceiling — its members could accumulate capital, but could not gain access to political power or obtain full legal protection in any of the states where they operated. For that class, the nation appears as the instrument that solves a practical problem: a state of its own that would protect its trade, recognize its contracts, and grant it status. Benedict Anderson described the general mechanism; the Greek case is one of its clearest examples.

The Peruvian parallel demands precision, because it is not identical. Peruvian independence was not driven by an eager criollo commercial bourgeoisie — Lima was the most loyal capital of the Spanish empire, with an elite that had prospered inside the commercial monopoly and that feared invading liberating armies almost as much as an indigenous rebellion, after the trauma of 1780. It came from outside, by sea: San Martín landed at Paracas in September 1820, Bolívar arrived in 1823, and the decisive battles of 1824 were fought by armies that were mostly not Peruvian. Greek independence and Peruvian independence thus share something more uncomfortable than a bourgeois origin: both arrived from the sea and from outside, sustained by external actors with their own agendas, imposed on populations that had not asked for them on those terms. What both inherited from that was a state that never quite came to coincide with its own society.

sections.heading: The Ionians: the other laboratory, 1797–1815
paragraphs: While this was happening in the Aegean and the Black Sea, the Ionian Islands passed through four different regimes in eighteen years, and that vertigo made them the first political laboratory of modern Greece.

In 1797 Napoleon dissolved the Republic of Venice, and the islands passed to France. The French did something in Corfu that will interest you in particular: they summoned the people to the Esplanade — the Spianada you will walk across — and publicly burned the LIBRO D'ORO, the Golden Book, the register of local nobility, planting a tree of liberty in its place. An act of revolutionary political theater of perfect eloquence: the ritual destruction of the document that constituted the social hierarchy. The hierarchies, of course, survived the burning of the register, as they usually do.

In 1799 a joint Russo-Ottoman fleet — circumstantial allies against France — expelled the French, and in 1800 the Septinsular Republic was created, formally independent under Ottoman sovereignty and Russian protection. It is considered the first modern Greek state, and it functioned for seven years amid constitutional disputes between nobles and commoners. In 1807 it returned to French hands, and in 1815, after the Congress of Vienna, it was constituted as the United States of the Ionian Islands under British protectorate, a regime that lasted until the cession to Greece in 1864.

That laboratory produced decisive figures: Ioannis Kapodistrias, a Corfiot, drafter of the Septinsular constitution, later foreign minister to the tsar and first head of state of independent Greece between 1828 and his assassination in 1831. And it also produced the Ionian Academy of Corfu, founded in 1824 under the British protectorate: the first university of modern Greece, twenty-five years ahead of any equivalent institution in Athens. When you reach the island, bear in mind that you are standing in a place that was the capital of a state before Athens was the capital of anything.

sections.heading: The loan as a form of independence
paragraphs: There is one last element, and it is the one that ties this block to the next. In 1824 and 1825, the revolutionary Greek government contracted two loans in London for a nominal amount of nearly two million eight hundred thousand pounds. After issue discounts, commissions, advance interest, and inflated purchases of matériel — including steamships that arrived late and in bad condition — Greece actually received around half that sum, perhaps less. The country went into default in 1827, before it even formally existed as a recognized state, and that debt shaped its foreign policy for decades.

Peru did the same thing at the same moment: the London loans of 1822 and 1825, contracted on onerous terms, with discounts that drastically reduced what was actually received, and default by around 1826. The two young nations were born indebted to the same financial center, in the same years, under structurally identical conditions.

This is the finding worth retaining from the whole of Block II: POLITICAL INDEPENDENCE WAS FINANCED WITH FINANCIAL DEPENDENCE, and the second long outlived the first. In the Greek case the circle closed in 1893 with bankruptcy and in 1898 with the International Financial Commission that administered Greek public revenues from abroad, and it closed again in 2010 with the memoranda. In the Peruvian case it closed with the guano crisis and the Grace Contract of 1889, which handed the railways over to British bondholders, and it closed again in the eighties and nineties. The instruments change; the structure — formal sovereignty, effective conditionality — is remarkably stable.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: the fleet that doesn't pay
paragraphs: The most literal continuity of this entrega is alive and quantifiable. Greek shipowners today control roughly a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage and nearly half the European Union's fleet: it is the largest fleet in the world by ownership, though most of those vessels sail under flags of convenience — Liberia, Panama, the Marshall Islands — which is to say, exactly what the Hydriots did under the Russian flag in 1774. Two hundred fifty years later, the strategy is identical: Greek capital, a foreign flag, a chosen jurisdiction.

And there is more. The Greek Constitution of 1975 devotes its Article 107 to protecting the special regime of shipping, and the sector is taxed by tonnage rather than profit, with the arrangement further recognized by the European Union. During the austerity years, while pensions were cut by twenty to forty percent, indirect taxes were raised, and youth unemployment exceeded fifty percent, the country's most profitable sector kept a privileged tax regime, offset by voluntary contributions negotiated in 2013 and renewed since. The fact does not call for indignant commentary; it calls for structural reading: a class that accumulated its capital outside the territory, and that can relocate it with a change of registry, holds a fiscal bargaining power that no salaried class possesses. The state taxes what cannot flee.

The Peruvian version is recognizable: tax-stability contracts in mining, avoidance through transfer pricing, and a tax burden that remains among the lowest in the region, around fifteen or sixteen percent of GDP, with more than two-thirds of employment informal. In both countries the conclusion is the same, and it is political, not technical: the adjustment falls on what cannot move — wages, consumption, pensions — because what can move negotiates. And in both countries public debate shifts toward the morality of the small taxpayer while the architecture that permits the flight remains untouched.
